Daily question

One question to sharpen the mind

Answer from instinct first, then read why. Getting it wrong here costs nothing — that is rather the point.

Think first

On the Moon, a hammer and a feather are dropped at the same moment from the same height. What happens?

On Earth the feather flutters down long after the hammer lands. The Moon has almost no atmosphere. So…

They land together. With no air resistance, every object accelerates toward the ground at the same rate, whatever its mass. Apollo 15 commander David Scott actually did this on live television in 1971 — hammer and falcon feather, one thud, same instant. Galileo had predicted it nearly 400 years earlier.

The toolkit

Six habits of a scientific mind

Not rules to win arguments — habits that keep your own thinking honest. Bring them into every thread and every call.

01

Ask “what's the evidence?”

Every claim carries a weight of proof. A screenshot is not a study; a confident tone is not data.

Try it: “Interesting — where was that measured, and by whom?”

02

Make it falsifiable

If no possible result could prove an idea wrong, it is not yet a scientific idea. Ask what would change your mind — then go looking for it.

Try it: “What observation would settle this between us?”

03

Correlation is not causation

Two things rising together may share a cause, cause each other, or be pure coincidence. Ice-cream sales and drowning both peak in summer; neither causes the other.

Try it: “What third factor could explain both?”

04

Prefer the simpler explanation

Occam's razor: between two explanations that fit the facts equally well, the one with fewer extra assumptions is usually the better bet — not a guarantee, a starting point.

Try it: “Does this need a conspiracy, or just a mistake?”

05

Steelman, don't strawman

Restate the other person's argument in its strongest form before answering it. If you can only beat the weak version, you have not beaten the idea.

Try it: “So your strongest point is… have I got that right?”

06

Update when the data changes

Changing your mind in the face of new evidence is not losing. It is the whole method. The only real failure is defending a position you no longer believe.

Try it: “I thought X — this study moves me to Y.”

House rules

How we treat each other here

Attack ideas, never people

“That claim doesn't hold up” is welcome. “You're an idiot” ends the conversation and helps no one learn.

Bring a source when you can

A paper, a dataset, a space-agency page. “I read somewhere” starts a search, not a conclusion.

Beginners are the point

No question is too basic. Everyone here once wondered the same thing and was lucky enough to be answered kindly.

Be safe on calls

Use a display name you're comfortable with, keep your camera off until you're ready, and never share personal details like your address or school.
